newsitem.title: INDIA: India cabinet approves plan for broadcast laws.
newsitem.headline: India cabinet approves plan for broadcast laws.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's cabinet on Tuesday approved a proposal for framing a comprehensive broadcasting law, a government spokesman said.

"The comprehensive broadcast law is expected to deal with issues relating to private broadcasting, setting up of an independent regulatory authority and making licences mandatory for all radio and television service providers," he said.
"Essentially it also says that no radio or television services can be provided without a licence," the spokesman said.
He said the bill would be introduced in parliament after it reconvened on Wednesday to discuss the passage of the 1997/98 (April-March) budget.
The spokesman said the cabinet also approved a proposal for amendments to the Prasar Bharati Bill which will provide autonomy to the state-run media, All India Radio and Doordarshan television.
The amendments to the Prasar Bharati Bill will also be introduced in the current session of parliament, the spokesman said. He gave no other details.
India began opening up key sectors under an economic liberalisation programme launched in 1991.

But the state still owns radio and television stations that broadcast from India, and there has been strong opposition to opening up broadcast media to the private sector, particularly foreign broadcasters.
The government leases out time-slots to private producers, but news programmes are subject to restrictions.

Dozens of time-slots are available to private producers with stipulated proportions of advertising time, but they cannot set up their own stations to air their programmes or acquire broadcast frequencies.
The government was pushed towards permitting private broadcasts in 1995, when the Supreme Court said that airwaves were public property and the state did not control a monopoly over them.
